planMarkdown:
Bot: Production-ready Telegram learning resource bot with private channel storage, Free/VIP access, admin uploads, tasks, and analytics

Summary:
Build a single-process Node.js ESM Telegram bot using grammY. The bot acts as a programming learning library where users browse resources through inline keyboards only. Content can be free or VIP-only. Admins upload files, links, text, media, or mixed messages through the bot, tag them by programming language/category, and the bot stores the actual Telegram message in a private storage channel while saving searchable metadata in MongoDB.

The bot supports VIP management by Telegram user ID, subscription expiry, renewal/removal, task-based VIP upgrades, countdown reminders, and automatic expiration handling. Admins can view user, content, VIP, task, and usage statistics from inline admin panels.

Product goals:
The bot should provide a clean learning-resource experience for programming students and developers. Users should be able to open the bot, browse categories, choose a programming language or topic, and receive files, links, notes, videos, archives, code snippets, PDFs, or other learning materials.

Core goals:

1) Store actual content inside a private Telegram channel controlled by the bot, so the bot can later copy or resend stored messages to users.

2) Use MongoDB as the catalog database for metadata such as title, description, language, tags, access level, storage channel message ID, upload date, uploader admin, file type, download count, and status.

3) Keep all user navigation inline. Main menu, category browsing, language browsing, content lists, pagination, VIP prompts, task actions, and admin controls should all use inline buttons.

4) Support Free and VIP access. Free users can access free resources. VIP users can access both free and VIP resources until their subscription expires.

5) Give admins full control through the bot: upload content, edit metadata, assign content to Free or VIP, add/remove VIP users, set subscription duration, create tasks, approve task completions, view statistics, and manage the language/category catalog.

6) Avoid trying to hardcode every programming language in the world into one giant keyboard. Instead, seed the bot with common programming languages and allow admins to add, rename, hide, or reorder languages/categories. This is more maintainable and prevents Telegram keyboard limits from becoming a problem.

7) Track useful analytics such as total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, content views/downloads, popular languages, VIP count, expired VIPs, task completions, and admin upload activity.

High-level architecture:
The bot runs as one Node.js ESM service using grammY. It has a modular internal design, but remains one process and does not require extra infrastructure beyond MongoDB and Telegram.

Main components:

1) Bot entrypoint: Initializes grammY with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, registers commands, callback query handlers, message handlers, admin flows, error handling, and graceful shutdown.

2) Routing layer: Separates user menu actions, admin menu actions, upload conversations, VIP management, task management, search/browse actions, and stats actions. All menu interactions use inline callback buttons.

3) Session and conversation layer: Tracks temporary admin upload steps, user search state, pagination state, task submission state, and admin VIP duration selection. Short-lived session data can be stored in memory, while important state should be persisted in MongoDB.

4) Access-control service: Determines whether a Telegram user is a normal user, VIP user, expired VIP user, or admin. Admin IDs should be configured from environment variables and may also be stored in MongoDB for secondary admin management if desired.

5) Content catalog service: Creates, updates, searches, lists, hides, restores, and deletes catalog records. Each record points to one or more Telegram storage channel message IDs.

6) Storage channel adapter: The bot must be added as an admin to the private storage channel. When an admin uploads content through the bot, the bot copies or posts that content into the private storage channel and stores the resulting channel message ID in MongoDB. When a user requests the content, the bot uses Telegram copy behavior to deliver the stored message to the user without exposing the channel as the main interface.

7) Admin upload pipeline: Admin starts upload, sends a file/message/link/media, then the bot asks for title, description, programming language/category, tags, access level, and optional notes. The bot saves the message to the storage channel, creates metadata in MongoDB, and confirms with inline buttons to preview, edit, publish, or cancel.

8) Inline menu engine: Generates paginated inline keyboards for main menu, languages, categories, resource lists, admin panels, stats pages, VIP controls, and task lists. This avoids huge keyboards and keeps the interface fast.

9) Subscription scheduler: A lightweight interval inside the same Node.js process checks VIP subscriptions periodically. It marks expired subscriptions, removes VIP access, and queues reminder messages before expiry. Because the service is single-process, these jobs should be idempotent and based on timestamps in MongoDB.

10) Analytics service: Records user starts, menu visits, searches, content opens, downloads/copies, task submissions, VIP changes, and admin uploads. Stats are aggregated from MongoDB and displayed in admin panels.

11) Error and audit logging: Important admin actions such as adding VIP, removing VIP, changing subscription duration, publishing content, deleting content, and approving tasks should be recorded in an audit collection. User-facing errors should be friendly, while internal errors should be logged for diagnosis.

Important Telegram requirements:

1) The private storage channel must exist before launch.

2) The bot must be an admin in the private storage channel with permission to post messages.

3) The channel ID should be configured securely through environment variables.

4) Users should not need to join the storage channel.

5) The bot should use copy/send behavior for delivery, not rely on users opening the private channel.

6) Large result lists must use pagination because Telegram inline keyboards and messages have practical size limits.

Data model:
MongoDB is the recommended persistence layer because this bot needs durable content records, VIP subscriptions, stats, task records, and admin audit logs. In-memory maps are only suitable for temporary sessions and small transient workflow state.

Recommended collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, lastName, languageCode, role, isBlocked, firstSeenAt, lastSeenAt, lastActiveAt, totalVisits, totalDownloads, source, createdAt, updatedAt.

2) vipsubscriptions
Fields: telegramUserId, status, startedAt, expiresAt, grantedByAdminId, durationDays, note, lastReminderAt, expiredAt, createdAt, updatedAt. Status values can include active, expired, cancelled, pending.

3) categories
Fields: name, slug, description, parentCategoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Examples: Programming Languages, Web Development, Mobile Development, Databases, DevOps, Cybersecurity, AI, Tools, Ebooks, Courses.

4) languages
Fields: name, slug, aliases, categoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Seed examples can include JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Dart, SQL, HTML, CSS, Bash, R, MATLAB, Lua, Scala, Perl, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Assembly, and others. Admins can add more later.

7) tasksubmissions

8) analyticsevents

Key flows:
User start and browsing flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record and logs a botstart event.

3) Bot shows an inline main menu: Browse Files, Search, Free Resources, VIP Resources, Tasks, My VIP Status, Help.

4) User chooses Browse Files.

5) Bot shows paginated categories and programming languages with inline buttons.

6) User chooses a language or category.

7) Bot shows paginated content items with inline buttons.

8) User selects a content item.

9) Bot checks access level. If free, it copies/sends the stored message from the private storage channel. If VIP-only, it verifies active VIP subscription before delivery.

10) Bot records contentviewed and contentdelivered analytics.

VIP access flow:

1) User opens VIP Resources or My VIP Status.

2) If user is not VIP, bot shows instructions to contact admin and provide their Telegram ID.

3) Bot displays the user’s Telegram ID clearly so they can copy it.

4) Admin uses Add VIP flow, enters the user ID, selects duration, adds optional note, and confirms.

5) Bot creates or updates vipsubscriptions with active status and expiresAt.

6) User receives a notification that VIP access is active, including expiry date and remaining time.

7) Before expiry, bot sends countdown reminders based on configured reminder timing.

8) After expiry, the scheduler marks the subscription expired and the user can no longer access VIP-only content.

Admin upload flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel through inline menu or /admin.

2) Admin selects Add Content.

3) Bot asks admin to send the resource. This can be a file, photo, video, audio, text, link, or document.

4) Bot receives the message and asks for title.

5) Bot asks for description.

6) Bot asks for category and programming language through paginated inline buttons, including an Add New Language option for admins.

7) Bot asks for tags as comma-separated text or selectable existing tags.

8) Bot asks whether the resource is Free or VIP.

9) Bot shows a confirmation preview.

10) On confirmation, bot copies/posts the content into the private storage channel, stores the channel message ID and metadata in MongoDB, publishes the content item, and shows management buttons: Preview, Edit, Hide, Add Another.

Admin VIP management flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel.

2) Admin selects VIP Users.

3) Admin chooses Add VIP, Remove VIP, Extend VIP, Shorten VIP, View Active VIP, View Expired VIP, or Find User.

4) For Add VIP, bot asks for Telegram user ID.

5) Bot asks subscription duration: preset inline buttons such as 1 day, 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, lifetime-style manual date, or custom days.

6) Bot confirms the target user and duration.

7) Bot saves the subscription and notifies the user if possible.

Task-to-VIP flow:

1) Admin creates a task with title, instructions, optional deadline, and VIP reward duration.

2) Users open Tasks from the main inline menu.

3) Bot lists active tasks.

4) User selects a task and submits proof as text, link, screenshot, file, or message depending on the task requirement.

5) Bot stores the submission and notifies admins.

6) Admin reviews pending submissions from the Admin Panel.

7) Admin approves or rejects with inline buttons.

8) If approved, bot automatically grants or extends VIP access according to the task reward.

Stats flow:

1) Admin opens Stats.

2) Bot shows quick totals: total users, active today, active this week, active this month, active VIP, expired VIP, total content, free content, VIP content, total downloads, tasks pending.

3) Admin can open deeper stats: user activity, content popularity, language popularity, VIP revenue/manual tracking notes if desired, task performance, upload activity, and admin audit logs.

4) Stats are computed from MongoDB records and analytics events.

Subscription expiry flow:

1) A periodic in-process checker scans active subscriptions with expiresAt in the past.

2) It marks them expired, records expiredAt, and logs an audit/system event.

3) It notifies the user that VIP access has ended and shows the inline button for renewal instructions.

4) A separate reminder scan checks subscriptions expiring soon and sends countdown reminders without spamming.

Tech stack:
Runtime and language:

1) Node.js using ECMAScript modules.

2) grammY as the Telegram bot framework.

3) TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN loaded from environment variables.

Persistence:

1) MongoDB for durable data: users, content metadata, VIP subscriptions, tasks, analytics, settings, and audit logs.

2) Simple in-memory maps may be used only for short-lived conversation/session state when losing that state on restart is acceptable.

3) No additional database, cache, message queue, or external worker system is required.

Storage:

1) The private Telegram channel is the primary content storage location for files, media, links, and messages.

2) MongoDB stores metadata and references to storage channel message IDs.

3) If temporary local handling is needed for generated exports or reports, use simple filesystem storage. If long-term non-Telegram binary storage is ever needed, describe it as object storage without tying the design to a specific vendor.

Deployment:

1) Run as a single Node.js server in the cloud.

2) The service can use long polling for simpler startup or webhook mode if the hosting environment provides a stable HTTPS endpoint.

3) Configuration should come from environment variables: TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN, MongoDB connection string, admin Telegram IDs, storage channel ID, and runtime mode.

Operational practices:

1) Centralized error handling inside the bot process.

2) Graceful shutdown for MongoDB connection and grammY bot stop behavior.

3) Idempotent scheduled checks for VIP expiry and reminders.

4) MongoDB indexes for performance.

5) Admin audit logs for sensitive operations.

Non-functional requirements:
Security:

1) Only configured admins can access admin panels and upload flows.

2) Admin actions must be validated at every callback, not only when rendering buttons.

3) User IDs entered for VIP management should be validated before saving.

4) The storage channel ID and bot token must never be shown to users.

5) The bot should avoid forwarding from the storage channel if channel identity should remain hidden; copy-style delivery is preferred.

Reliability:

1) All important records should be saved in MongoDB before confirming success to admins.

2) Upload flow should support cancellation and recovery from invalid input.

3) Scheduled expiry and reminder jobs should be safe to run repeatedly.

4) If Telegram delivery fails because the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and continue.

Performance:

1) Use pagination for languages, categories, content lists, users, and stats.

2) Use indexed queries for content search and VIP checks.

3) Avoid loading all files or users into memory.

4) Keep callback payloads short by storing state in MongoDB or session records and referencing compact IDs.

Maintainability:

1) Separate services internally: user service, content service, VIP service, task service, stats service, storage channel service, and admin service.

2) Keep all messages and button labels in a configurable text/settings layer so the bot can be edited without changing business logic.

3) Use consistent callback naming conventions.

4) Keep language/category lists admin-manageable instead of hardcoding everything forever.

Compliance and content quality:

1) Admins should only upload content they have permission to distribute.

2) VIP/free labeling should be clear before users request content.

3) The bot should support hiding or deleting content records if files become outdated, broken, or inappropriate.

4) Add reporting or feedback buttons so users can report broken files or request new resources.

Bot commands:
• /start — Starts the bot, registers or updates the user, and shows the main inline menu. (usage: /start) [user]
• /menu — Returns the user to the main inline menu with browsing, VIP, tasks, and help options. (usage: /menu) [user]
• /id — Shows the user their Telegram ID so they can send it to an admin for VIP activation. (usage: /id) [user]
• /vip — Shows VIP status, expiry countdown, and instructions for getting or renewing VIP access. (usage: /vip) [user]
• /tasks — Opens the active task list where users can complete tasks to request or earn VIP access. (usage: /tasks) [user]
• /help — Shows help, usage instructions, support information, and basic rules. (usage: /help) [user]
• /admin — Opens the admin control panel for authorized admins only. (usage: /admin) [admin]
• /add — Starts the admin content upload flow for saving a new file, link, media item, or message into the storage channel and catalog. (usage: /add) [admin]
• /vipadmin — Opens VIP management for adding, removing, extending, shortening, or finding VIP users. (usage: /vipadmin) [admin]
• /stats — Shows admin-only bot statistics including users, activity, content, downloads, VIP users, and tasks. (usage: /stats) [admin]
• /broadcast — Starts an admin broadcast flow for sending announcements to users, with confirmation and safe delivery tracking. (usage: /broadcast) [admin]
• /cancel — Cancels the current multi-step user or admin flow and returns to the relevant menu. (usage: /cancel) [shared]

DOCS.md.content:
Code Vault is a Telegram bot for sharing programming learning resources through inline menus.

It stores original files, links, text posts, and media in a private Telegram storage channel. MongoDB stores searchable metadata, users, VIP subscriptions, tasks, submissions, activity events, and stats.

Public commands:

1) /start
Opens Code Vault, registers or refreshes the user, records a visit, checks sponsor membership when configured, and shows the inline main menu.

2) /help
Explains how to browse free files, request VIP access, submit tasks, and use the admin contact flow.

Main menu buttons:

1) Browse Files
Shows programming languages and categories with inline buttons. The default categories include JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Ruby, Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin, Dart, HTML, CSS, SQL, Shell/Bash, Lua, R, MATLAB, Solidity, Web3, DevOps, Databases, Frameworks, Tools, Ebooks, Courses, Templates, and Other.

2) Search
Lets users search resource titles, descriptions, tags, and categories.

3) Free Files
Shows free resources available to all registered users.

4) VIP Files
Shows VIP resources. Free users can view metadata but cannot receive the stored file until VIP is active.

5) My VIP Status
Shows whether the user is Free or VIP. VIP users see expiry date and remaining time. Free users see VIP instructions and their Telegram user ID.

6) Tasks
Shows active tasks created by admins. Users can submit proof as text, file, image, media, or link.

7) Help
Shows usage instructions.

8) Admin Panel
Visible only to admins configured in BOT_ADMIN_IDS.

Admin panel sections:

1) Upload Resource
Starts an upload wizard. The admin sends a file, media, link, or text post. The bot asks for title, description, category/language, tags, Free or VIP tier, and confirmation. After confirmation, the bot copies the content to STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID and stores metadata in MongoDB.

2) Manage Resources
Lists recent resources and allows admins to hide or delete records.

3) VIP Users
Admins can add, extend, inspect, list, and remove VIP users by Telegram user ID. Durations include 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, lifetime, and custom days.

4) Tasks
Admins can create active tasks and review pending submissions. Approval can grant VIP days when the task has a VIP reward.

5) Stats
Shows total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, visits, deliveries, failed deliveries, total resources, resources by tier, resources by category, active/expired VIP users, task counts, and task submission counts.

6) Settings/Help
Shows runtime configuration guidance.

Private storage channel setup:

1) Create a private Telegram channel.

2) Add the bot as an admin in that channel.

3) Give the bot permission to post messages.

4) Get the channel ID. Private channel IDs usually look like -1001234567890.

5) Set STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID to that ID.

6) Do not add the storage channel to sponsor requirements. It is only for private content storage.

Admin setup:

1) Get your Telegram numeric user ID.

2) Set BOT_ADMIN_IDS to a comma-separated list, for example 11111111,22222222.

3) If BOT_ADMIN_IDS is empty, the bot still starts, logs a warning, and hides admin features.

VIP behavior:

Free users can receive free resources.

VIP resources require an active VIP subscription. VIP is checked when opening VIP areas and again immediately before delivery.

Expired subscriptions are marked expired by an in-process scheduled loop. Lifetime VIP subscriptions do not expire automatically.

If VIP_CONTACT_TEXT is not configured, the bot falls back to a generic instruction asking the user to message an admin with their Telegram user ID.

Sponsor join gate:

If SPONSOR_CHAT_IDS is configured, non-admin users must be members of those channels/groups before accessing menus. This should include sponsor or backup groups/channels only, never the private storage channel.

Use SPONSOR_JOIN_URLS to show join buttons. The bot checks membership with Telegram getChatMember.

MongoDB collections:

1) users
Stores Telegram user profile, first seen, last active, visit count, and download count.

2) resources
Stores title, description, category, tags, tier, storage channel ID, storage message ID, status, views, downloads, and failed delivery count.

3) vipSubscriptions
Stores Telegram user ID, status, start date, expiry date, lifetime flag, grantedBy admin ID, duration, and notes.

4) tasks
Stores task title, instructions, reward type, VIP reward days, status, and creator admin.

5) taskSubmissions
Stores task ID, user ID, submitted message ID/text, review status, reviewer, review note, and timestamps.

6) activityEvents
Stores visits, menu opens, searches, file views, delivery success/failure, task views, and submissions.

7) categories
Stores configurable programming languages/categories.

Environment variables:

1) TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN
Required. Bot token from BotFather.

2) MONGODB_URI
Required for full operation. Used for users, catalog, VIPs, tasks, and stats.

3) STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID
Required for uploads and file delivery. Must point to the private storage channel.

4) BOT_ADMIN_IDS
Required for admin features. Comma-separated numeric Telegram user IDs.

5) VIP_CONTACT_TEXT
Optional. Custom text shown to free users requesting VIP.

6) DEFAULT_VIP_DAYS
Optional. Defaults to 30.

7) SPONSOR_CHAT_IDS
Optional. Comma-separated sponsor chat IDs users must join before access.

8) SPONSOR_JOIN_URLS
Optional. Comma-separated invite/public URLs used as join buttons.

9) VIP_EXPIRY_CHECK_MS
Optional. Defaults to 300000.

Run locally:

1) Install dependencies with npm install.

2) Copy .env.sample to .env.

3) Fill TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, MONGODB_URI, STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID, and BOT_ADMIN_IDS.

4) Run npm run dev.

Deploy as one Node.js service:

1) Set the same environment variables in your hosting panel.

2) Build command: npm run build.

3) Start command: npm start.

4) The bot uses long polling and clears webhooks before polling.

Diagnostics:

The bot logs boot env sanity using booleans only. It never logs secrets.

It logs MongoDB connection failures, storage channel copy operations, upload start/success/failure, delivery start/success/failure, fallback attempts, polling failures, VIP expiry loop cycles, and memory usage once per minute.

state.planMarkdown:
Bot: Production-ready Telegram learning resource bot with private channel storage, Free/VIP access, admin uploads, tasks, and analytics

Summary:
Build a single-process Node.js ESM Telegram bot using grammY. The bot acts as a programming learning library where users browse resources through inline keyboards only. Content can be free or VIP-only. Admins upload files, links, text, media, or mixed messages through the bot, tag them by programming language/category, and the bot stores the actual Telegram message in a private storage channel while saving searchable metadata in MongoDB.

The bot supports VIP management by Telegram user ID, subscription expiry, renewal/removal, task-based VIP upgrades, countdown reminders, and automatic expiration handling. Admins can view user, content, VIP, task, and usage statistics from inline admin panels.

Product goals:
The bot should provide a clean learning-resource experience for programming students and developers. Users should be able to open the bot, browse categories, choose a programming language or topic, and receive files, links, notes, videos, archives, code snippets, PDFs, or other learning materials.

Core goals:

1) Store actual content inside a private Telegram channel controlled by the bot, so the bot can later copy or resend stored messages to users.

2) Use MongoDB as the catalog database for metadata such as title, description, language, tags, access level, storage channel message ID, upload date, uploader admin, file type, download count, and status.

3) Keep all user navigation inline. Main menu, category browsing, language browsing, content lists, pagination, VIP prompts, task actions, and admin controls should all use inline buttons.

4) Support Free and VIP access. Free users can access free resources. VIP users can access both free and VIP resources until their subscription expires.

5) Give admins full control through the bot: upload content, edit metadata, assign content to Free or VIP, add/remove VIP users, set subscription duration, create tasks, approve task completions, view statistics, and manage the language/category catalog.

6) Avoid trying to hardcode every programming language in the world into one giant keyboard. Instead, seed the bot with common programming languages and allow admins to add, rename, hide, or reorder languages/categories. This is more maintainable and prevents Telegram keyboard limits from becoming a problem.

7) Track useful analytics such as total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, content views/downloads, popular languages, VIP count, expired VIPs, task completions, and admin upload activity.

High-level architecture:
The bot runs as one Node.js ESM service using grammY. It has a modular internal design, but remains one process and does not require extra infrastructure beyond MongoDB and Telegram.

Main components:

1) Bot entrypoint: Initializes grammY with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, registers commands, callback query handlers, message handlers, admin flows, error handling, and graceful shutdown.

2) Routing layer: Separates user menu actions, admin menu actions, upload conversations, VIP management, task management, search/browse actions, and stats actions. All menu interactions use inline callback buttons.

3) Session and conversation layer: Tracks temporary admin upload steps, user search state, pagination state, task submission state, and admin VIP duration selection. Short-lived session data can be stored in memory, while important state should be persisted in MongoDB.

4) Access-control service: Determines whether a Telegram user is a normal user, VIP user, expired VIP user, or admin. Admin IDs should be configured from environment variables and may also be stored in MongoDB for secondary admin management if desired.

5) Content catalog service: Creates, updates, searches, lists, hides, restores, and deletes catalog records. Each record points to one or more Telegram storage channel message IDs.

6) Storage channel adapter: The bot must be added as an admin to the private storage channel. When an admin uploads content through the bot, the bot copies or posts that content into the private storage channel and stores the resulting channel message ID in MongoDB. When a user requests the content, the bot uses Telegram copy behavior to deliver the stored message to the user without exposing the channel as the main interface.

7) Admin upload pipeline: Admin starts upload, sends a file/message/link/media, then the bot asks for title, description, programming language/category, tags, access level, and optional notes. The bot saves the message to the storage channel, creates metadata in MongoDB, and confirms with inline buttons to preview, edit, publish, or cancel.

8) Inline menu engine: Generates paginated inline keyboards for main menu, languages, categories, resource lists, admin panels, stats pages, VIP controls, and task lists. This avoids huge keyboards and keeps the interface fast.

9) Subscription scheduler: A lightweight interval inside the same Node.js process checks VIP subscriptions periodically. It marks expired subscriptions, removes VIP access, and queues reminder messages before expiry. Because the service is single-process, these jobs should be idempotent and based on timestamps in MongoDB.

10) Analytics service: Records user starts, menu visits, searches, content opens, downloads/copies, task submissions, VIP changes, and admin uploads. Stats are aggregated from MongoDB and displayed in admin panels.

11) Error and audit logging: Important admin actions such as adding VIP, removing VIP, changing subscription duration, publishing content, deleting content, and approving tasks should be recorded in an audit collection. User-facing errors should be friendly, while internal errors should be logged for diagnosis.

Important Telegram requirements:

1) The private storage channel must exist before launch.

2) The bot must be an admin in the private storage channel with permission to post messages.

3) The channel ID should be configured securely through environment variables.

4) Users should not need to join the storage channel.

5) The bot should use copy/send behavior for delivery, not rely on users opening the private channel.

6) Large result lists must use pagination because Telegram inline keyboards and messages have practical size limits.

Data model:
MongoDB is the recommended persistence layer because this bot needs durable content records, VIP subscriptions, stats, task records, and admin audit logs. In-memory maps are only suitable for temporary sessions and small transient workflow state.

Recommended collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, lastName, languageCode, role, isBlocked, firstSeenAt, lastSeenAt, lastActiveAt, totalVisits, totalDownloads, source, createdAt, updatedAt.

2) vipsubscriptions
Fields: telegramUserId, status, startedAt, expiresAt, grantedByAdminId, durationDays, note, lastReminderAt, expiredAt, createdAt, updatedAt. Status values can include active, expired, cancelled, pending.

3) categories
Fields: name, slug, description, parentCategoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Examples: Programming Languages, Web Development, Mobile Development, Databases, DevOps, Cybersecurity, AI, Tools, Ebooks, Courses.

4) languages
Fields: name, slug, aliases, categoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Seed examples can include JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Dart, SQL, HTML, CSS, Bash, R, MATLAB, Lua, Scala, Perl, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Assembly, and others. Admins can add more later.

5) contentitems
Fields: title, description, contentType, accessLevel, categoryId, languageId, tags, storageChatId, storageMessageIds, originalUploaderAdminId, status, fileName, fileSize, mimeType, telegramFileId, previewText, publishedAt, createdAt, updatedAt, viewCount, downloadCount, lastAccessedAt. Access level values: free, vip. Status values: draft, published, hidden, deleted.

6) tasks
Fields: title, description, instructions, rewardType, rewardVipDays, status, createdByAdminId, startsAt, endsAt, maxApprovals, createdAt, updatedAt. Status values: active, paused, ended.

7) tasksubmissions
Fields: taskId, telegramUserId, submissionText, submissionMessageIds, status, reviewedByAdminId, reviewNote, submittedAt, reviewedAt. Status values: pending, approved, rejected.

8) analyticsevents
Fields: telegramUserId, eventType, metadata, createdAt. Event examples: botstart, menuopened, categoryopened, languageopened, contentviewed, contentdelivered, vippromptopened, taskopened, tasksubmitted, adminuploadstarted, admincontentpublished.

9) adminauditlogs
Fields: adminTelegramUserId, action, targetType, targetId, details, createdAt. This gives traceability for sensitive actions.

10) settings
Fields: key, value, updatedByAdminId, updatedAt. Useful for welcome text, VIP instruction text, support/admin contact text, reminder schedule, and default subscription durations.

Indexes to plan:

1) users.telegramUserId unique.

2) vipsubscriptions.telegramUserId and vipsubscriptions.status.

3) vipsubscriptions.expiresAt for expiry checks.

4) contentitems.status, accessLevel, categoryId, languageId, tags.

5) analyticsevents.createdAt and analyticsevents.eventType.

6) tasksubmissions.taskId, telegramUserId, status.

7) languages.slug and categories.slug unique.

Key flows:
User start and browsing flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record and logs a botstart event.

3) Bot shows an inline main menu: Browse Files, Search, Free Resources, VIP Resources, Tasks, My VIP Status, Help.

4) User chooses Browse Files.

5) Bot shows paginated categories and programming languages with inline buttons.

6) User chooses a language or category.

7) Bot shows paginated content items with inline buttons.

8) User selects a content item.

9) Bot checks access level. If free, it copies/sends the stored message from the private storage channel. If VIP-only, it verifies active VIP subscription before delivery.

10) Bot records contentviewed and contentdelivered analytics.

VIP access flow:

1) User opens VIP Resources or My VIP Status.

2) If user is not VIP, bot shows instructions to contact admin and provide their Telegram ID.

3) Bot displays the user’s Telegram ID clearly so they can copy it.

4) Admin uses Add VIP flow, enters the user ID, selects duration, adds optional note, and confirms.

5) Bot creates or updates vipsubscriptions with active status and expiresAt.

6) User receives a notification that VIP access is active, including expiry date and remaining time.

7) Before expiry, bot sends countdown reminders based on configured reminder timing.

8) After expiry, the scheduler marks the subscription expired and the user can no longer access VIP-only content.

Admin upload flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel through inline menu or /admin.

2) Admin selects Add Content.

3) Bot asks admin to send the resource. This can be a file, photo, video, audio, text, link, or document.

4) Bot receives the message and asks for title.

planSections.productGoals:
The bot should provide a clean learning-resource experience for programming students and developers. Users should be able to open the bot, browse categories, choose a programming language or topic, and receive files, links, notes, videos, archives, code snippets, PDFs, or other learning materials.

Core goals:

1) Store actual content inside a private Telegram channel controlled by the bot, so the bot can later copy or resend stored messages to users.

2) Use MongoDB as the catalog database for metadata such as title, description, language, tags, access level, storage channel message ID, upload date, uploader admin, file type, download count, and status.

3) Keep all user navigation inline. Main menu, category browsing, language browsing, content lists, pagination, VIP prompts, task actions, and admin controls should all use inline buttons.

4) Support Free and VIP access. Free users can access free resources. VIP users can access both free and VIP resources until their subscription expires.

5) Give admins full control through the bot: upload content, edit metadata, assign content to Free or VIP, add/remove VIP users, set subscription duration, create tasks, approve task completions, view statistics, and manage the language/category catalog.

6) Avoid trying to hardcode every programming language in the world into one giant keyboard. Instead, seed the bot with common programming languages and allow admins to add, rename, hide, or reorder languages/categories. This is more maintainable and prevents Telegram keyboard limits from becoming a problem.

7) Track useful analytics such as total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, content views/downloads, popular languages, VIP count, expired VIPs, task completions, and admin upload activity.
planSections.highLevelArchitecture:
The bot runs as one Node.js ESM service using grammY. It has a modular internal design, but remains one process and does not require extra infrastructure beyond MongoDB and Telegram.

Main components:

1) Bot entrypoint: Initializes grammY with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, registers commands, callback query handlers, message handlers, admin flows, error handling, and graceful shutdown.

2) Routing layer: Separates user menu actions, admin menu actions, upload conversations, VIP management, task management, search/browse actions, and stats actions. All menu interactions use inline callback buttons.

3) Session and conversation layer: Tracks temporary admin upload steps, user search state, pagination state, task submission state, and admin VIP duration selection. Short-lived session data can be stored in memory, while important state should be persisted in MongoDB.

4) Access-control service: Determines whether a Telegram user is a normal user, VIP user, expired VIP user, or admin. Admin IDs should be configured from environment variables and may also be stored in MongoDB for secondary admin management if desired.

5) Content catalog service: Creates, updates, searches, lists, hides, restores, and deletes catalog records. Each record points to one or more Telegram storage channel message IDs.

6) Storage channel adapter: The bot must be added as an admin to the private storage channel. When an admin uploads content through the bot, the bot copies or posts that content into the private storage channel and stores the resulting channel message ID in MongoDB. When a user requests the content, the bot uses Telegram copy behavior to deliver the stored message to the user without exposing the channel as the main interface.

7) Admin upload pipeline: Admin starts upload, sends a file/message/link/media, then the bot asks for title, description, programming language/category, tags, access level, and optional notes. The bot saves the message to the storage channel, creates metadata in MongoDB, and confirms with inline buttons to preview, edit, publish, or cancel.

8) Inline menu engine: Generates paginated inline keyboards for main menu, languages, categories, resource lists, admin panels, stats pages, VIP controls, and task lists. This avoids huge keyboards and keeps the interface fast.

9) Subscription scheduler: A lightweight interval inside the same Node.js process checks VIP subscriptions periodically. It marks expired subscriptions, removes VIP access, and queues reminder messages before expiry. Because the service is single-process, these jobs should be idempotent and based on timestamps in MongoDB.

10) Analytics service: Records user starts, menu visits, searches, content opens, downloads/copies, task submissions, VIP changes, and admin uploads. Stats are aggregated from MongoDB and displayed in admin panels.

11) Error and audit logging: Important admin actions such as adding VIP, removing VIP, changing subscription duration, publishing content, deleting content, and approving tasks should be recorded in an audit collection. User-facing errors should be friendly, while internal errors should be logged for diagnosis.

Important Telegram requirements:

1) The private storage channel must exist before launch.

2) The bot must be an admin in the private storage channel with permission to post messages.

3) The channel ID should be configured securely through environment variables.

4) Users should not need to join the storage channel.

5) The bot should use copy/send behavior for delivery, not rely on users opening the private channel.

6) Large result lists must use pagination because Telegram inline keyboards and messages have practical size limits.

DOCS.md.content:
Code Vault is a Telegram bot for sharing programming learning resources through inline menus.

It stores original files, links, text posts, and media in a private Telegram storage channel. MongoDB stores searchable metadata, users, VIP subscriptions, tasks, submissions, activity events, and stats.

Public commands:

1) /start
Opens Code Vault, registers or refreshes the user, records a visit, checks sponsor membership when configured, and shows the inline main menu.

2) /help
Explains how to browse free files, request VIP access, submit tasks, and use the admin contact flow.

Main menu buttons:

1) Browse Files
Shows programming languages and categories with inline buttons. The default categories include JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Ruby, Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin, Dart, HTML, CSS, SQL, Shell/Bash, Lua, R, MATLAB, Solidity, Web3, DevOps, Databases, Frameworks, Tools, Ebooks, Courses, Templates, and Other.

2) Search
Lets users search resource titles, descriptions, tags, and categories.

3) Free Files
Shows free resources available to all registered users.

4) VIP Files
Shows VIP resources. Free users can view metadata but cannot receive the stored file until VIP is active.

5) My VIP Status
Shows whether the user is Free or VIP. VIP users see expiry date and remaining time. Free users see VIP instructions and their Telegram user ID.

6) Tasks
Shows active tasks created by admins. Users can submit proof as text, file, image, media, or link.

7) Help
Shows usage instructions.

8) Admin Panel
Visible only to admins configured in BOT_ADMIN_IDS.

Admin panel sections:

1) Upload Resource
Starts an upload wizard. The admin sends a file, media, link, or text post. The bot asks for title, description, category/language, tags, Free or VIP tier, and confirmation. After confirmation, the bot copies the content to STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID and stores metadata in MongoDB.

2) Manage Resources
Lists recent resources and allows admins to hide or delete records.

3) VIP Users
Admins can add, extend, inspect, list, and remove VIP users by Telegram user ID. Durations include 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, lifetime, and custom days.

4) Tasks
Admins can create active tasks and review pending submissions. Approval can grant VIP days when the task has a VIP reward.

5) Stats
Shows total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, visits, deliveries, failed deliveries, total resources, resources by tier, resources by category, active/expired VIP users, task counts, and task submission counts.

6) Settings/Help
Shows runtime configuration guidance.

Private storage channel setup:

1) Create a private Telegram channel.

2) Add the bot as an admin in that channel.

3) Give the bot permission to post messages.

4) Get the channel ID. Private channel IDs usually look like -1001234567890.

5) Set STORAGE_CHANNEL_ID to that ID.

6) Do not add the storage channel to sponsor requirements. It is only for private content storage.

Admin setup:

1) Get your Telegram numeric user ID.

2) Set BOT_ADMIN_IDS to a comma-separated list, for example 11111111,22222222.

3) If BOT_ADMIN_IDS is empty, the bot still starts, logs a warning, and hides admin features.

VIP behavior:

Free users can receive free resources.

VIP resources require an active VIP subscription. VIP is checked when opening VIP areas and again immediately before delivery.

Expired subscriptions are marked expired by an in-process scheduled loop. Lifetime VIP subscriptions do not expire automatically.

If VIP_CONTACT_TEXT is not configured, the bot falls back to a generic instruction asking the user to message an admin with their Telegram user ID.

Sponsor join gate:

If SPONSOR_CHAT_IDS is configured, non-admin users must be members of those channels/groups before accessing menus. This should include sponsor or backup groups/channels only, never the private storage channel.

Use SPONSOR_JOIN_URLS to show join buttons. The bot checks membership with Telegram getChatMember.

MongoDB collections:

1) users
Stores Telegram user profile, first seen, last active, visit count, and download count.

2) resources
Stores title, description, category, tags, tier, storage channel ID, storage message ID, status, views, downloads, and failed delivery count.

3) vipSubscriptions
Stores Telegram user ID, status, start date, expiry date, lifetime flag, grantedBy admin ID, duration, and notes.

4) tasks
Stores task title, instructions, reward type, VIP reward days, status, and creator admin.

5) taskSubmissions
Stores task ID, user ID, submitted message ID/text, review status, reviewer, review note, and timestamps.

6) activityEvents
Stores visits, menu opens, searches, file views, delivery success/failure, task views, and submissions.

7) categories
Stores configurable programming languages/categories.

Environment variables:

state.planMarkdown:
Bot: Production-ready Telegram learning resource bot with private channel storage, Free/VIP access, admin uploads, tasks, and analytics

Summary:
Build a single-process Node.js ESM Telegram bot using grammY. The bot acts as a programming learning library where users browse resources through inline keyboards only. Content can be free or VIP-only. Admins upload files, links, text, media, or mixed messages through the bot, tag them by programming language/category, and the bot stores the actual Telegram message in a private storage channel while saving searchable metadata in MongoDB.

The bot supports VIP management by Telegram user ID, subscription expiry, renewal/removal, task-based VIP upgrades, countdown reminders, and automatic expiration handling. Admins can view user, content, VIP, task, and usage statistics from inline admin panels.

Product goals:
The bot should provide a clean learning-resource experience for programming students and developers. Users should be able to open the bot, browse categories, choose a programming language or topic, and receive files, links, notes, videos, archives, code snippets, PDFs, or other learning materials.

Core goals:

1) Store actual content inside a private Telegram channel controlled by the bot, so the bot can later copy or resend stored messages to users.

2) Use MongoDB as the catalog database for metadata such as title, description, language, tags, access level, storage channel message ID, upload date, uploader admin, file type, download count, and status.

3) Keep all user navigation inline. Main menu, category browsing, language browsing, content lists, pagination, VIP prompts, task actions, and admin controls should all use inline buttons.

4) Support Free and VIP access. Free users can access free resources. VIP users can access both free and VIP resources until their subscription expires.

5) Give admins full control through the bot: upload content, edit metadata, assign content to Free or VIP, add/remove VIP users, set subscription duration, create tasks, approve task completions, view statistics, and manage the language/category catalog.

6) Avoid trying to hardcode every programming language in the world into one giant keyboard. Instead, seed the bot with common programming languages and allow admins to add, rename, hide, or reorder languages/categories. This is more maintainable and prevents Telegram keyboard limits from becoming a problem.

7) Track useful analytics such as total users, active users daily/weekly/monthly, content views/downloads, popular languages, VIP count, expired VIPs, task completions, and admin upload activity.

High-level architecture:
The bot runs as one Node.js ESM service using grammY. It has a modular internal design, but remains one process and does not require extra infrastructure beyond MongoDB and Telegram.

Main components:

1) Bot entrypoint: Initializes grammY with TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN from environment variables, registers commands, callback query handlers, message handlers, admin flows, error handling, and graceful shutdown.

2) Routing layer: Separates user menu actions, admin menu actions, upload conversations, VIP management, task management, search/browse actions, and stats actions. All menu interactions use inline callback buttons.

3) Session and conversation layer: Tracks temporary admin upload steps, user search state, pagination state, task submission state, and admin VIP duration selection. Short-lived session data can be stored in memory, while important state should be persisted in MongoDB.

4) Access-control service: Determines whether a Telegram user is a normal user, VIP user, expired VIP user, or admin. Admin IDs should be configured from environment variables and may also be stored in MongoDB for secondary admin management if desired.

5) Content catalog service: Creates, updates, searches, lists, hides, restores, and deletes catalog records. Each record points to one or more Telegram storage channel message IDs.

6) Storage channel adapter: The bot must be added as an admin to the private storage channel. When an admin uploads content through the bot, the bot copies or posts that content into the private storage channel and stores the resulting channel message ID in MongoDB. When a user requests the content, the bot uses Telegram copy behavior to deliver the stored message to the user without exposing the channel as the main interface.

7) Admin upload pipeline: Admin starts upload, sends a file/message/link/media, then the bot asks for title, description, programming language/category, tags, access level, and optional notes. The bot saves the message to the storage channel, creates metadata in MongoDB, and confirms with inline buttons to preview, edit, publish, or cancel.

8) Inline menu engine: Generates paginated inline keyboards for main menu, languages, categories, resource lists, admin panels, stats pages, VIP controls, and task lists. This avoids huge keyboards and keeps the interface fast.

9) Subscription scheduler: A lightweight interval inside the same Node.js process checks VIP subscriptions periodically. It marks expired subscriptions, removes VIP access, and queues reminder messages before expiry. Because the service is single-process, these jobs should be idempotent and based on timestamps in MongoDB.

10) Analytics service: Records user starts, menu visits, searches, content opens, downloads/copies, task submissions, VIP changes, and admin uploads. Stats are aggregated from MongoDB and displayed in admin panels.

11) Error and audit logging: Important admin actions such as adding VIP, removing VIP, changing subscription duration, publishing content, deleting content, and approving tasks should be recorded in an audit collection. User-facing errors should be friendly, while internal errors should be logged for diagnosis.

Important Telegram requirements:

1) The private storage channel must exist before launch.

2) The bot must be an admin in the private storage channel with permission to post messages.

3) The channel ID should be configured securely through environment variables.

4) Users should not need to join the storage channel.

5) The bot should use copy/send behavior for delivery, not rely on users opening the private channel.

6) Large result lists must use pagination because Telegram inline keyboards and messages have practical size limits.

Data model:
MongoDB is the recommended persistence layer because this bot needs durable content records, VIP subscriptions, stats, task records, and admin audit logs. In-memory maps are only suitable for temporary sessions and small transient workflow state.

Recommended collections:

1) users
Fields: telegramUserId, username, firstName, lastName, languageCode, role, isBlocked, firstSeenAt, lastSeenAt, lastActiveAt, totalVisits, totalDownloads, source, createdAt, updatedAt.

2) vipsubscriptions
Fields: telegramUserId, status, startedAt, expiresAt, grantedByAdminId, durationDays, note, lastReminderAt, expiredAt, createdAt, updatedAt. Status values can include active, expired, cancelled, pending.

3) categories
Fields: name, slug, description, parentCategoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Examples: Programming Languages, Web Development, Mobile Development, Databases, DevOps, Cybersecurity, AI, Tools, Ebooks, Courses.

4) languages
Fields: name, slug, aliases, categoryId, sortOrder, isVisible, createdByAdminId, createdAt, updatedAt. Seed examples can include JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, C, C++, C#, Go, Rust, PHP, Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Dart, SQL, HTML, CSS, Bash, R, MATLAB, Lua, Scala, Perl, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Assembly, and others. 5) contentitems

Access level values: free, vip. Status values: draft, published, hidden, deleted.

6) tasks
Fields: title, description, instructions, rewardType, rewardVipDays, status, createdByAdminId, startsAt, endsAt, maxApprovals, createdAt, updatedAt. Status values: active, paused, ended.

7) tasksubmissions
Fields: taskId, telegramUserId, submissionText, submissionMessageIds, status, reviewedByAdminId, reviewNote, submittedAt, reviewedAt. Status values: pending, approved, rejected.

8) analyticsevents
Fields: telegramUserId, eventType, metadata, createdAt. Event examples: botstart, menuopened, categoryopened, languageopened, contentviewed, contentdelivered, vippromptopened, taskopened, tasksubmitted, adminuploadstarted, admincontentpublished.

9) adminauditlogs
Fields: adminTelegramUserId, action, targetType, targetId, details, createdAt. This gives traceability for sensitive actions.

10) settings

Indexes to plan:

1) users.telegramUserId unique.

2) vipsubscriptions.telegramUserId and vipsubscriptions.status.

3) vipsubscriptions.expiresAt for expiry checks.

4) contentitems.status, accessLevel, categoryId, languageId, tags.

5) analyticsevents.createdAt and analyticsevents.eventType.

6) tasksubmissions.taskId, telegramUserId, status.

7) languages.slug and categories.slug unique.

Key flows:
User start and browsing flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record and logs a botstart event.

3) Bot shows an inline main menu: Browse Files, Search, Free Resources, VIP Resources, Tasks, My VIP Status, Help.

4) User chooses Browse Files.

5) Bot shows paginated categories and programming languages with inline buttons.

6) User chooses a language or category.

7) Bot shows paginated content items with inline buttons.

8) User selects a content item.

9) Bot checks access level. If free, it copies/sends the stored message from the private storage channel. If VIP-only, it verifies active VIP subscription before delivery.

10) Bot records contentviewed and contentdelivered analytics.

VIP access flow:

1) User opens VIP Resources or My VIP Status.

2) If user is not VIP, bot shows instructions to contact admin and provide their Telegram ID.

3) Bot displays the user’s Telegram ID clearly so they can copy it.

4) Admin uses Add VIP flow, enters the user ID, selects duration, adds optional note, and confirms.

5) Bot creates or updates vipsubscriptions with active status and expiresAt.

6) User receives a notification that VIP access is active, including expiry date and remaining time.

7) Before expiry, bot sends countdown reminders based on configured reminder timing.

8) After expiry, the scheduler marks the subscription expired and the user can no longer access VIP-only content.

Admin upload flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel through inline menu or /admin.

2) Admin selects Add Content.

3) Bot asks admin to send the resource. This can be a file, photo, video, audio, text, link, or document.

4) Bot receives the message and asks for title.

5) Bot asks for description.

6) Bot asks for category and programming language through paginated inline buttons, including an Add New Language option for admins.

7) Bot asks for tags as comma-separated text or selectable existing tags.

8) Bot asks whether the resource is Free or VIP.

9) Bot shows a confirmation preview.

10) On confirmation, bot copies/posts the content into the private storage channel, stores the channel message ID and metadata in MongoDB, publishes the content item, and shows management buttons: Preview, Edit, Hide, Add Another.

Admin VIP management flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel.

2) Admin selects VIP Users.

3) Admin chooses Add VIP, Remove VIP, Extend VIP, Shorten VIP, View Active VIP, View Expired VIP, or Find User.

4) For Add VIP, bot asks for Telegram user ID.

5) Bot asks subscription duration: preset inline buttons such as 1 day, 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, lifetime-style manual date, or custom days.

6) Bot confirms the target user and duration.

7) Bot saves the subscription and notifies the user if possible.

Task-to-VIP flow:

1) Admin creates a task with title, instructions, optional deadline, and VIP reward duration.

2) Users open Tasks from the main inline menu.

3) Bot lists active tasks.

4) User selects a task and submits proof as text, link, screenshot, file, or message depending on the task requirement.

5) Bot stores the submission and notifies admins.

6) Admin reviews pending submissions from the Admin Panel.

7) Admin approves or rejects with inline buttons.

8) If approved, bot automatically grants or extends VIP access according to the task reward.

Stats flow:

1) Admin opens Stats.

2) Bot shows quick totals: total users, active today, active this week, active this month, active VIP, expired VIP, total content, free content, VIP content, total downloads, tasks pending.

3) Admin can open deeper stats: user activity, content popularity, language popularity, VIP revenue/manual tracking notes if desired, task performance, upload activity, and admin audit logs.

4) Stats are computed from MongoDB records and analytics events.

Subscription expiry flow:

1) A periodic in-process checker scans active subscriptions with expiresAt in the past.

2) It marks them expired, records expiredAt, and logs an audit/system event.

3) It notifies the user that VIP access has ended and shows the inline button for renewal instructions.

4) A separate reminder scan checks subscriptions expiring soon and sends countdown reminders without spamming.

Tech stack:
Runtime and language:

1) Node.js using ECMAScript modules.

2) grammY as the Telegram bot framework.

3) TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN loaded from environment variables.

Persistence:

1) MongoDB for durable data: users, content metadata, VIP subscriptions, tasks, analytics, settings, and audit logs.

2) Simple in-memory maps may be used only for short-lived conversation/session state when losing that state on restart is acceptable.

3) No additional database, cache, message queue, or external worker system is required.

Storage:

1) The private Telegram channel is the primary content storage location for files, media, links, and messages.

2) MongoDB stores metadata and references to storage channel message IDs.

3) If temporary local handling is needed for generated exports or reports, use simple filesystem storage. If long-term non-Telegram binary storage is ever needed, describe it as object storage without tying the design to a specific vendor.

Deployment:

1) Run as a single Node.js server in the cloud.

2) The service can use long polling for simpler startup or webhook mode if the hosting environment provides a stable HTTPS endpoint.

3) Configuration should come from environment variables: TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN, MongoDB connection string, admin Telegram IDs, storage channel ID, and runtime mode.

Operational practices:

1) Centralized error handling inside the bot process.

2) Graceful shutdown for MongoDB connection and grammY bot stop behavior.

3) Idempotent scheduled checks for VIP expiry and reminders.

4) MongoDB indexes for performance.

5) Admin audit logs for sensitive operations.

Non-functional requirements:
Security:

1) Only configured admins can access admin panels and upload flows.

2) Admin actions must be validated at every callback, not only when rendering buttons.

3) User IDs entered for VIP management should be validated before saving.

4) The storage channel ID and bot token must never be shown to users.

5) The bot should avoid forwarding from the storage channel if channel identity should remain hidden; copy-style delivery is preferred.

Reliability:

1) All important records should be saved in MongoDB before confirming success to admins.

2) Upload flow should support cancellation and recovery from invalid input.

3) Scheduled expiry and reminder jobs should be safe to run repeatedly.

4) If Telegram delivery fails because the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and continue.

Performance:

1) Use pagination for languages, categories, content lists, users, and stats.

2) Use indexed queries for content search and VIP checks.

3) Avoid loading all files or users into memory.

4) Keep callback payloads short by storing state in MongoDB or session records and referencing compact IDs.

Maintainability:

1) Separate services internally: user service, content service, VIP service, task service, stats service, storage channel service, and admin service.

2) Keep all messages and button labels in a configurable text/settings layer so the bot can be edited without changing business logic.

3) Use consistent callback naming conventions.

4) Keep language/category lists admin-manageable instead of hardcoding everything forever.

Compliance and content quality:

1) Admins should only upload content they have permission to distribute.

2) VIP/free labeling should be clear before users request content.

3) The bot should support hiding or deleting content records if files become outdated, broken, or inappropriate.

4) Add reporting or feedback buttons so users can report broken files or request new resources.

Bot commands:
• /start — Starts the bot, registers or updates the user, and shows the main inline menu. (usage: /start) [user]
• /menu — Returns the user to the main inline menu with browsing, VIP, tasks, and help options. (usage: /menu) [user]
• /id — Shows the user their Telegram ID so they can send it to an admin for VIP activation. (usage: /id) [user]
• /vip — Shows VIP status, expiry countdown, and instructions for getting or renewing VIP access. (usage: /vip) [user]
• /tasks — Opens the active task list where users can complete tasks to request or earn VIP access. (usage: /tasks) [user]
• /help — Shows help, usage instructions, support information, and basic rules. (usage: /help) [user]
• /admin — Opens the admin control panel for authorized admins only. (usage: /admin) [admin]
• /add — Starts the admin content upload flow for saving a new file, link, media item, or message into the storage channel and catalog. (usage: /add) [admin]
• /vipadmin — Opens VIP management for adding, removing, extending, shortening, or finding VIP users. (usage: /vipadmin) [admin]
• /stats — Shows admin-only bot statistics including users, activity, content, downloads, VIP users, and tasks. (usage: /stats) [admin]
• /broadcast — Starts an admin broadcast flow for sending announcements to users, with confirmation and safe delivery tracking. (usage: /broadcast) [admin]
• /cancel — Cancels the current multi-step user or admin flow and returns to the relevant menu. (usage: /cancel) [shared]

planSections.keyFlows:
User start and browsing flow:

1) User sends /start.

2) Bot creates or updates the user record and logs a botstart event.

3) Bot shows an inline main menu: Browse Files, Search, Free Resources, VIP Resources, Tasks, My VIP Status, Help.

4) User chooses Browse Files.

5) Bot shows paginated categories and programming languages with inline buttons.

6) User chooses a language or category.

7) Bot shows paginated content items with inline buttons.

8) User selects a content item.

9) Bot checks access level. If free, it copies/sends the stored message from the private storage channel. If VIP-only, it verifies active VIP subscription before delivery.

10) Bot records contentviewed and contentdelivered analytics.

VIP access flow:

1) User opens VIP Resources or My VIP Status.

2) If user is not VIP, bot shows instructions to contact admin and provide their Telegram ID.

3) Bot displays the user’s Telegram ID clearly so they can copy it.

4) Admin uses Add VIP flow, enters the user ID, selects duration, adds optional note, and confirms.

5) Bot creates or updates vipsubscriptions with active status and expiresAt.

6) User receives a notification that VIP access is active, including expiry date and remaining time.

7) Before expiry, bot sends countdown reminders based on configured reminder timing.

8) After expiry, the scheduler marks the subscription expired and the user can no longer access VIP-only content.

Admin upload flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel through inline menu or /admin.

2) Admin selects Add Content.

3) Bot asks admin to send the resource. This can be a file, photo, video, audio, text, link, or document.

4) Bot receives the message and asks for title.

5) Bot asks for description.

6) Bot asks for category and programming language through paginated inline buttons, including an Add New Language option for admins.

7) Bot asks for tags as comma-separated text or selectable existing tags.

8) Bot asks whether the resource is Free or VIP.

9) Bot shows a confirmation preview.

10) On confirmation, bot copies/posts the content into the private storage channel, stores the channel message ID and metadata in MongoDB, publishes the content item, and shows management buttons: Preview, Edit, Hide, Add Another.

Admin VIP management flow:

1) Admin opens Admin Panel.

2) Admin selects VIP Users.

3) Admin chooses Add VIP, Remove VIP, Extend VIP, Shorten VIP, View Active VIP, View Expired VIP, or Find User.

4) For Add VIP, bot asks for Telegram user ID.

5) Bot asks subscription duration: preset inline buttons such as 1 day, 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, lifetime-style manual date, or custom days.

6) Bot confirms the target user and duration.

7) Bot saves the subscription and notifies the user if possible.

Task-to-VIP flow:

1) Admin creates a task with title, instructions, optional deadline, and VIP reward duration.

2) Users open Tasks from the main inline menu.

3) Bot lists active tasks.

4) User selects a task and submits proof as text, link, screenshot, file, or message depending on the task requirement.

5) Bot stores the submission and notifies admins.

6) Admin reviews pending submissions from the Admin Panel.

7) Admin approves or rejects with inline buttons.

8) If approved, bot automatically grants or extends VIP access according to the task reward.

Stats flow:

1) Admin opens Stats.

2) Bot shows quick totals: total users, active today, active this week, active this month, active VIP, expired VIP, total content, free content, VIP content, total downloads, tasks pending.

3) Admin can open deeper stats: user activity, content popularity, language popularity, VIP revenue/manual tracking notes if desired, task performance, upload activity, and admin audit logs.

4) Stats are computed from MongoDB records and analytics events.

Subscription expiry flow:

1) A periodic in-process checker scans active subscriptions with expiresAt in the past.

2) It marks them expired, records expiredAt, and logs an audit/system event.

3) It notifies the user that VIP access has ended and shows the inline button for renewal instructions.

4) A separate reminder scan checks subscriptions expiring soon and sends countdown reminders without spamming.
planSections.techStack:
Runtime and language:

1) Node.js using ECMAScript modules.

2) grammY as the Telegram bot framework.

3) TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN loaded from environment variables.

Persistence:

1) MongoDB for durable data: users, content metadata, VIP subscriptions, tasks, analytics, settings, and audit logs.

2) Simple in-memory maps may be used only for short-lived conversation/session state when losing that state on restart is acceptable.

3) No additional database, cache, message queue, or external worker system is required.

Storage:

1) The private Telegram channel is the primary content storage location for files, media, links, and messages.

2) MongoDB stores metadata and references to storage channel message IDs.

3) If temporary local handling is needed for generated exports or reports, use simple filesystem storage. If long-term non-Telegram binary storage is ever needed, describe it as object storage without tying the design to a specific vendor.

Deployment:

1) Run as a single Node.js server in the cloud.

2) The service can use long polling for simpler startup or webhook mode if the hosting environment provides a stable HTTPS endpoint.

3) Configuration should come from environment variables: TELEGRAMBOTTOKEN, MongoDB connection string, admin Telegram IDs, storage channel ID, and runtime mode.

Operational practices:

1) Centralized error handling inside the bot process.

2) Graceful shutdown for MongoDB connection and grammY bot stop behavior.

3) Idempotent scheduled checks for VIP expiry and reminders.

4) MongoDB indexes for performance.

5) Admin audit logs for sensitive operations.
planSections.nonFunctional:
Security:

1) Only configured admins can access admin panels and upload flows.

2) Admin actions must be validated at every callback, not only when rendering buttons.

3) User IDs entered for VIP management should be validated before saving.

4) The storage channel ID and bot token must never be shown to users.

5) The bot should avoid forwarding from the storage channel if channel identity should remain hidden; copy-style delivery is preferred.

Reliability:

1) All important records should be saved in MongoDB before confirming success to admins.

2) Upload flow should support cancellation and recovery from invalid input.

3) Scheduled expiry and reminder jobs should be safe to run repeatedly.

4) If Telegram delivery fails because the user blocked the bot, mark the user as blocked and continue.

Performance:

1) Use pagination for languages, categories, content lists, users, and stats.

2) Use indexed queries for content search and VIP checks.

3) Avoid loading all files or users into memory.

4) Keep callback payloads short by storing state in MongoDB or session records and referencing compact IDs.

Maintainability:

1) Separate services internally: user service, content service, VIP service, task service, stats service, storage channel service, and admin service.

2) Keep all messages and button labels in a configurable text/settings layer so the bot can be edited without changing business logic.

3) Use consistent callback naming conventions.

4) Keep language/category lists admin-manageable instead of hardcoding everything forever.

Compliance and content quality:

1) Admins should only upload content they have permission to distribute.

2) VIP/free labeling should be clear before users request content.

3) The bot should support hiding or deleting content records if files become outdated, broken, or inappropriate.

4) Add reporting or feedback buttons so users can report broken files or request new resources.
